title: Convert a `List<Employee>` back into a `List<String>` of CSV rows (reverse of the above).
shortTitle: Convert a List<Employee> back into a List<String> of CSV rows (reverse of the above)

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This is a serialising `map` that turns each structured `Employee` back into a single CSV line, joining its fields with the delimiter. The mapping function formats the name, department, and salary into one comma-separated string, so the stream goes from `Stream<Employee>` to `Stream<String>`.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The clerk at the National Bank of India now has filled employee forms and must send them back out as plain text, one line per person like "Rajesh,IT,95000". She reads each form and writes its fields on a line separated by commas. `map` doing the join-into-a-line is exactly that flattening of a form back into text.

**One line to remember:** `map` can serialise each object into a CSV row by joining its fields with commas.

sections.s2_technical:
The mapping function takes an Employee and returns one CSV string. The simplest form joins the fields directly, for example `e -> e.getName() + "," + e.getDepartment() + "," + e.getSalary()`. Each employee produces exactly one line, so it is one-to-one, and the stream's element type becomes String.

For money the salary is a BigDecimal, and calling toString on it gives a clean decimal text like 95000 or 95000.00, depending on its scale. If a fixed format is required, for example always two decimal places, you format it explicitly with `salary.toPlainString()` or a `DecimalFormat`, because toPlainString avoids scientific notation that a very large BigDecimal could otherwise produce.

A robust serialiser also considers escaping. If any field could contain the delimiter itself — a department like "Sales, North" — a naive join would produce a broken row with too many columns. Proper CSV wraps such fields in quotes and escapes internal quotes, which again is why a real CSV library is preferable when fields are not guaranteed delimiter-free. For clean, controlled internal data a direct join is acceptable.

A senior nuance: serialisation and parsing should be symmetric and tested together with a round-trip test — parse then serialise should reproduce the original line, and serialise then parse should reproduce the original object. That round-trip property is the quickest way to catch a formatting or escaping bug before it corrupts an export.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India must send a nightly export back to a partner system that only accepts plain CSV, so every Employee object in memory has to become one comma-separated line like "Rajesh,IT,95000". This is exactly how a serialising map works — each employee is turned into a single CSV row by joining its fields with commas, with the salary rendered as a plain decimal.

The code defines an `Employee` with name, department and a `BigDecimal` salary. A `CsvExportService` exposes `toCsvRows(List<Employee>)` that maps each employee to a CSV line. The runnable `Main` feeds employees and logs the exported rows.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three Employee objects — Rajesh (IT, 95000), Priya (Sales, 72000), Amit (HR, 48000).

Step 1: The stream opens over three structured employees.

Step 2: Rajesh flows into map. The function reads his name, department, and salary; the salary BigDecimal is rendered with toPlainString as 95000; the three pieces are joined with commas into the line "Rajesh,IT,95000".

Step 3: Priya becomes "Priya,Sales,72000".

Step 4: Amit becomes "Amit,HR,48000".

Step 5: The stream's element type is now String, with three elements because map is one-to-one.

Step 6: `collect` gathers the three CSV lines into a list, ready to be written to the export file.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: Stream<Employee> [Rajesh{IT,95000}, Priya{Sales,72000}, Amit{HR,48000}]
    │
    ▼
  map(e -> name + "," + dept + "," + salary.toPlainString())
    ├─ Rajesh{IT,95000}   → "Rajesh,IT,95000"
    ├─ Priya{Sales,72000} → "Priya,Sales,72000"
    └─ Amit{HR,48000}     → "Amit,HR,48000"
    │  (type Employee → String, one-to-one)
    ▼
  collect(toList())  →  List<String> CSV rows → write to export file
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — CSV Serialising map ═══

  ┌─ Serialisation rules ────────────────────────────────┐
  │ join fields with "," → one row per employee          │
  │ salary.toPlainString() → no scientific notation      │
  │ escape fields containing "," (use library if risky)  │
  │ round-trip test: parse(serialise(x)) == x            │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────┐ reads ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │   CsvExportService   │──────▶│        Employee           │
  │ ──────────────────── │       │ - name, department        │
  │ + toCsvRows(List)    │       │ - salary: BigDecimal      │
  │     : List<String>   │       └──────────────────────────┘
  └──────────────────────┘

  Contract for toCsvRows:
    Pre:  list non-null, fields non-null
    Post: one "name,department,salary" row per employee
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
To serialise structured objects back into CSV I use a map whose function joins each object's fields with commas into a single line, so the stream goes from a stream of employees to a stream of strings, one row per employee, which I collect into a list ready to write to a file. For the salary, which is a BigDecimal, I render it with toPlainString so the output never slips into scientific notation that a very large number could otherwise produce.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India this was the nightly export to a partner system that only accepts plain CSV, so every employee object in memory had to become one comma-separated line. It is the exact reverse of the import, turning structured data back into text.

A senior point I always make is that serialisation and parsing must be symmetric and tested together with a round-trip test: parsing a line and serialising it again should reproduce the original line, and serialising an object and parsing it back should reproduce the original object. That round-trip property is the fastest way to catch a formatting bug before it corrupts a real export. I also watch for the escaping trap — if a field could contain the delimiter itself, like a department written as Sales comma North, a naive join produces a broken row with too many columns, so for data that is not guaranteed delimiter-free I use a proper CSV library that handles quoting and escaping rather than a hand-rolled join.
